author: Paul Kennedy
biz: Size the fixed commitments against the base that funds them

Kennedy's overstretch is a cost structure problem. This week, list every standing monthly commitment across Ruby Holdings, the broker brands and Debt Support Direct, and set the total beside the lowest monthly gross profit of the past twelve months rather than the average. Anything the worst month cannot carry is overstretch, however good the good months look. Measure the ratio of fixed cost to worst month gross profit, and track it monthly. A falling ratio is the only reliable sign the business is getting stronger rather than merely busier.
Watch the leading ledger, not the lagging one

Kennedy's point is that the base shifts years before the headline event. Applied to lead generation, approvals and completions are lagging numbers. This week pick three leading ones and chart them weekly: cost per qualified enquiry by source, the proportion of enquiries where the customer's stated need is genuinely suited to a secured loan, and first contact answer rate. Falling suitability with rising volume is the warning Kennedy would recognise, and it is also the Consumer Duty signal that matters, since advertising reach must never outrun the ability to serve customers well.

b: Paul Michael Kennedy was born on the seventeenth of June 1945, in Wallsend, on the north bank of the Tyne. He arrived about five weeks after the war in Europe ended, in a town whose name and whose trade both pointed backwards to things that were ending. Wallsend sits at the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall, the place where one empire looked north and decided it had gone far enough. And it was a shipbuilding town, which in 1945 still meant a great deal, and within forty years would mean almost nothing at all.

The yard that dominated the place was Swan Hunter. In 1906 it had launched the Mauretania, for years the fastest liner on the Atlantic. Through two world wars its slipways had turned out warships and merchant hulls on a scale that is hard to picture now. A child walking those streets in the late 1940s looked up and saw steel hulls the height of churches standing on blocks at the end of ordinary terraced roads, with cranes above the chimney pots. It would have been entirely reasonable for that child to assume this was simply what Britain was. The country that made the ships.
He was educated at Saint Cuthbert's Grammar School in Newcastle, up the hill from the river, and then at the University of Newcastle.

Within his own lifetime the yards along that river would empty, one by one, and the cranes would come down. The question that runs underneath everything Paul Kennedy later wrote is the question a boy from Wallsend would naturally ask. Not why a country loses a battle. How a country that builds the world's ships stops being able to.

b: In 1966, the year he took a first in history at Newcastle, Kennedy got a job a young historian today would barely dare to imagine. He became research assistant to Sir Basil Liddell Hart, and he held the post for four years, until 1970, drafting chapters for Liddell Hart's enormous History of the Second World War.

Liddell Hart was then the most famous military thinker writing in English. He had spent decades arguing that the proper object of strategy is not the enemy army but the enemy's will and capacity, and that the direct assault is usually the most expensive route to either. To sit at his desk in your early twenties, sorting his papers and drafting his sentences, was an education in reading war from the inside.

At the same time Kennedy was writing a doctorate at Saint Antony's College, Oxford, which he finished in 1970. His supervisors were two of the most formidable historians in Britain. One was A. J. P. Taylor, the great and quarrelsome historian of European diplomacy, who believed history was told in archives and narrative, not theory. The other was John Gallagher, who with Ronald Robinson had reshaped the whole study of empire by arguing that the formal, coloured in parts of the map were only the visible tip of something mostly economic, and that Britain had often preferred influence to ownership because influence was cheaper.

So the young man had three teachers, and each of them owned a different piece of the puzzle. Liddell Hart had the fighting. Taylor had the diplomacy. Gallagher had the money and the trade. Almost everything Kennedy went on to write is an attempt to refuse to keep those three things in separate rooms.

b: In 1970 Kennedy joined the history department at the University of East Anglia, where he stayed for thirteen years, rising from lecturer to reader in 1975 and to professor in 1982. His first books were careful and narrow. There was a pair of volumes on the Pacific war, then in 1974 The Samoan Tangle, a study of a small imperial squabble in the South Seas.

Then in 1976 he published the book that contains the seed of everything else. The Rise and Fall of British Naval Mastery asked how the Royal Navy came to rule the oceans and how it stopped. The conventional answer was a story of admirals, tactics and ships. Kennedy's answer was a story of coal, iron, shipyards, credit, trade routes and relative industrial weight. The Navy had been supreme, he argued, because for a stretch of history Britain had been the workshop and the banker of the world, and when other countries industrialised, the supremacy drained away whatever the Admiralty did about it.

That book introduced the idea he would hammer at for the rest of his life. Power is relative. A country can grow richer every year and become weaker every year at the same time, if others are growing faster. Nothing has to go wrong for a great power to decline. Other people merely have to go right.

In 1980 he published The Rise of the Anglo-German Antagonism, covering the years 1860 to 1914, a study of how two advanced, related, heavily armed countries talked themselves into a collision. He was becoming the historian of the slow fuse rather than the explosion.

b: When Kennedy finally sat down to write the big book, he began in 1500, and he began with a case that ought to have been easy. The Habsburg dynasty, in the century and a half from 1519 to 1659, controlled Spain, much of Italy, the Low Countries, Austria, and the silver of the New World. On paper it was the richest power Europe had seen. It made a serious bid for mastery of the continent, and it did not get there.

Kennedy's handling of that failure is the most interesting thing in the early part of the book, because he refuses to make it look inevitable. The Habsburgs were not hopeless. They very nearly managed it. Everyone involved was exhausted, including the Dutch republic that resisted them, and he describes the eventual outcome as a marginal and relative victory rather than a triumph. What defeated the silver was simple arithmetic. The commitments were in too many places at once, armies had grown enormous, and no treasure fleet arrives often enough to pay for a war on four frontiers.

Then he moved to the period from 1660 to 1815, and found the mechanism that mattered. Britain, in that long duel with France, spent roughly two and a quarter billion pounds on its wars. Tax and revenue brought in only about one and three quarter billion. The gap, something close to a third of everything it spent, was borrowed, through the Bank of England and the funded national debt.

That is the insight dressed as an accounting note. Britain did not usually win because it had better soldiers. It won because it could borrow at a lower rate for longer than its rivals could, and a state that can borrow cheaply can lose battles and still win wars.

b: The second half of the book changes instrument. For the pre industrial world Kennedy had to work with tax receipts, troop numbers and the judgement of contemporaries. For the industrial era he had something better. He had output.

Leaning on the calculations of the economic historian Paul Bairoch, he set British industrial production per head in 1900 at one hundred, and then showed the climb. Britain stood at ten in 1750, sixteen in 1800, twenty five in 1830, sixty four in 1860, eighty seven in 1880, and one hundred in 1900. France over the same century and a half went from nine to thirty nine. Two countries, one island apart, pulling steadily out of each other's reach.

The share of world manufacturing output is more startling still, because it runs the other way. In 1750 China produced getting on for a third of everything manufactured on earth, somewhere near thirty three parts in a hundred. By 1860 that was under twenty, and by 1880 it was about twelve and a half. Britain in the same stretch went from under two parts in a hundred to nearly twenty three.

Nothing in those numbers is a battle. The Opium Wars and the Taiping rebellion sit inside that Chinese collapse, but the collapse is wider and quieter than any of them. And this is Kennedy's real claim, the one worth carrying away. The economic ledger moves first, often decades before anybody fires a shot, and the political and military shock that follows is the world catching up with a change that has already happened.

b: The two central chapters of the book cover the years 1885 to 1918 and then 1919 to 1942, and Kennedy gives them both the same subtitle. The coming of a bipolar world and the crisis of the middle powers.

That phrase is the hinge of the whole argument. By the end of the nineteenth century it was becoming clear that the future belonged to continental scale states, the United States and Russia, with their populations, coal, grain and internal markets. And it was becoming clear to the countries that currently held great power rank, Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Austria Hungary, that their base would not carry that rank for very much longer.

A country in that position has three choices, all of them bad. It can accept demotion, which no governing class has ever found easy. It can try to buy its way back by acquiring more, which means colonies, markets, dependencies, and collisions with everyone else doing the same thing. Or it can gamble on a short decisive war while it still has an army good enough to win one.

Kennedy's two world wars are, at bottom, the resolution of that squeeze. Germany in 1914 and again in 1939 is the clearest case of a middle power attempting to force a continental base into existence before the window shut. Britain's interwar problem is the mirror image, a country holding a quarter of the world with an economy that could no longer pay for the garrisons. He is not saying economics caused the wars. He is saying it set the table at which the decisions were taken.

b: In 1983 Kennedy left East Anglia for Yale, where he was appointed the J. Richardson Dilworth Professor of History. Four years later, in 1987, Random House published The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers, with the subtitle Economic Change and Military Conflict from 1500 to 2000. It ran to six hundred and seventy seven pages and carried twelve maps, forty nine tables and three charts. It was his eighth book and it swallowed the other seven.

The engine of the argument is a triangle. Every state has to divide its resources between guns, butter and investment. Guns are defence. Butter is what the population expects to be given now. Investment is the future productive base. A rising power can afford to be generous to all three because the pie is growing. A declining power has to rob one to feed the others, and whichever it robs, it pays for later.

What makes the squeeze worse over time is that the cost of weapons rises faster than the cost of anything else. Kennedy gives the figures that make the point stick. A battleship before 1914 cost something in the order of two and a half million pounds. A frigate in the 1980s, a far smaller ship, ran to something nearer one hundred and twenty million. Military power does not get cheaper as technology improves. It gets dearer, relentlessly, and the share of national income needed to stay in the same place keeps climbing.

From that he drew the phrase everybody remembers. Imperial overstretch. The condition of a state whose strategic commitments have grown larger than the economy underneath them, so that the very effort of defending its position accelerates the erosion of it. And in the final chapter he turned the diagnosis on the United States.

b: A six hundred page economic history of five centuries is not supposed to be a bestseller. This one was. It reached number six on the hardcover bestseller list for 1988, won the Wolfson History Prize, and has since been translated into more than twenty languages.

The reviews from inside the trade were generous and, in one case, rather moving. A. J. P. Taylor, who had supervised the young man's doctorate eighteen years earlier, called it an encyclopaedia in itself. Sir Michael Howard, the dean of British military history, called it a deeply humane book in the very best sense of the word.

Outside the trade it landed in the middle of an argument that Americans were already having with themselves. The 1980s had brought a huge defence build up, a federal deficit to match, and the uncomfortable sight of a country that had been the world's largest creditor becoming its largest debtor. Kennedy's comparison between the American network of overseas bases and the British one before 1914 was quoted everywhere. American Heritage magazine ran a cover question in September 1988 asking whether America was falling behind. The word declinism entered political speech, and Kennedy, a careful Tyneside historian, found himself cast as the prophet of American decay in an election year.

He had been careful, in fact. His advice was not that America was finished. It was that a power in relative decline should manage the erosion slowly and intelligently rather than pretend it is not happening or try to spend its way out.

b: Two years after publication the Berlin Wall opened. Two years after that the Soviet Union dissolved. The Cold War did not end in the slow mutual exhaustion the book implied. It ended with one of the two superpowers simply ceasing to exist, and the other emerging without a rival anywhere on earth.

For about a decade this was treated as the refutation of Paul Kennedy. It was the opposite. If you want a textbook case of a state whose strategic commitments devoured the economy that was meant to support them, the Soviet Union of the 1980s is the finest example of the twentieth century. Kennedy had described the mechanism correctly and been slightly wrong about which patient would show the symptoms first, and that is a different kind of error from being wrong about how the disease works.

He did get things wrong, and he has been straightforward about it. He expected Japan to keep rising, and Japanese growth stalled after 1990 and never resumed. He was right about China, strikingly so, noting that Deng Xiaoping's four modernisations deliberately put the military behind the economy, which was precisely the choice his own thesis would recommend. Critics pushed back on deeper ground. Henry Nau argued in 2001 that the model gives too little weight to national identity, to democratic institutions, and to the possibility that countries which trade and vote together stop competing in the old way at all.

Kennedy's own criticism of his book is the sharpest of the lot. It is, he has said, somewhat deterministic, because it does not focus on the individual, the creative spark, or the creative moment. His later Engineers of Victory, published in 2013, reads like a deliberate answer to that charge, a book about the problem solvers who turned material advantage into actual results.

b: Kennedy stayed at Yale, directing its International Security Studies programme. He was made a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2001 and a Fellow of the British Academy in 2003. He went on writing: Preparing for the Twenty-first Century in 1993, The Parliament of Man in 2006 on the United Nations, Engineers of Victory in 2013, and in 2022 Victory at Sea, a return to the warships he had grown up beside.

The river did not do as well. Shipbuilding on the Tyne contracted through the 1970s and 1980s, Swan Hunter went through nationalisation, sale and administration, and in the end the work stopped. In 2007 the yard's giant cranes, the ones that had stood over the Wallsend rooftops, were sold to a shipbuilder in India and taken down. The slipways where the Mauretania was launched are quiet.

It is worth saying plainly. The man who explained how the economic base under a great power can shift for decades before anybody notices the consequences had watched exactly that process happen to his own home town, at child's eye level, from the inside.

That is what the book is for. Not prophecy, because prophecy is the part Kennedy got wrong. It is a way of looking. Before you ask who has the best army or the loudest politics, ask what is actually being produced, by whom, and at what cost, and ask whether the promises a country has made are larger than the thing paying for them. The answer tends to be visible years early, written in output and interest rates rather than in headlines, for countries and for anything else that has to keep its commitments smaller than its means.

recall: Who did Paul Kennedy work for between 1966 and 1970, and what was he doing?

He was research assistant to Sir Basil Liddell Hart, the most famous military thinker then writing in English. He drafted chapters for Liddell Hart's History of the Second World War while simultaneously writing his Oxford doctorate.
What does imperial overstretch mean in Kennedy's sense?

It is the condition of a state whose strategic commitments have grown larger than the economy that has to pay for them. The effort of defending its position then accelerates the erosion of that position.
What do the British war finance figures from 1688 to 1815 show?

Britain spent roughly two and a quarter billion pounds on its wars but raised only about one and three quarter billion in revenue. Close to a third was borrowed, which made cheap credit, not better soldiers, the decisive British advantage.
What happened to China's share of world manufacturing output between 1750 and 1880?
It fell from roughly a third of everything manufactured on earth to about twelve and a half parts in a hundred. Britain in the same period rose from under two to nearly twenty three.
Why did the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 look like a refutation of Kennedy's book, and why was it not?

The book was read as predicting American decline, so the United States emerging as sole superpower looked like an error. But the Soviet Union was itself the clearest case of commitments devouring an economic base, so the mechanism he described was confirmed even though he had the patient wrong.
recap:
Paul Kennedy was born in Wallsend on the Tyne in June 1945, five weeks after the war in Europe ended, in a shipbuilding town where hulls the height of churches stood on blocks at the end of terraced streets. Within his lifetime those yards would empty. The question that shaped his career was not why a country loses a battle, but how a country that builds the world's ships stops being able to.

He took a first at Newcastle in 1966, then spent four years as research assistant to Sir Basil Liddell Hart, drafting chapters of his history of the Second World War, while writing an Oxford doctorate under A. J. P. Taylor and John Gallagher. Fighting, diplomacy and money, three teachers and three pieces of one puzzle. In 1976 he put them together in The Rise and Fall of British Naval Mastery, arguing that the Royal Navy ruled the sea because Britain was the workshop and banker of the world, and stopped ruling it when others industrialised.

The big book came in 1987, from Yale: six hundred and seventy seven pages, forty nine tables, five centuries. Four ideas carry it.

First, power is relative. A country can grow richer every year and weaker every year at the same time, because others are growing faster. Nothing has to go wrong.

Second, the economic ledger moves first. China produced about a third of the world's manufactures in 1750 and twelve and a half parts in a hundred by 1880, and that collapse is wider and quieter than any war inside it.

Third, credit is a weapon. Britain spent roughly two and a quarter billion pounds on its wars between 1688 and 1815 and borrowed close to a third of it. It won because it could borrow cheaply for longer, not because its soldiers were better.

Fourth, imperial overstretch. Guns, butter and investment compete for the same pound, the price of weapons rises faster than everything else, and a state whose commitments outgrow its base erodes itself by the very act of defending its position.

Then the Soviet Union collapsed and he looked wrong, until you notice it was the purest case of his own thesis. He misjudged the patient, not the disease. His own verdict on the book was that it was too deterministic and left too little room for the creative moment.

The cranes over Wallsend came down in 2007 and were shipped to India. Before you ask who has the best army, ask what is being produced, by whom, at what cost, and whether the promises are bigger than the thing paying for them.
stories: The silver that was not enough

For a century and a half the Habsburgs held Spain, much of Italy, the Low Countries, Austria and the silver mines of the New World. On paper it was the strongest hand anybody in Europe had been dealt. They made a serious bid for mastery of the continent and never closed it out. Kennedy's explanation is not that they were badly led, but that the commitments were in too many places at once and armies had grown enormous. No treasure fleet arrives often enough to pay for a war on four frontiers. The richest power in Europe lost to its own diary.
Two and a half million pounds, then one hundred and twenty

Kennedy wanted to show that military power gets dearer rather than cheaper, so he picked two ships. A battleship before 1914, the most formidable machine on earth at the time, cost something near two and a half million pounds. A frigate in the 1980s, a considerably smaller vessel, cost nearer one hundred and twenty million. The weapons improve and the price per unit of security rises anyway. It follows that a country holding its defence budget flat is not standing still. It is retreating slowly, in good order, and calling it prudence.
The prophet proved right by the wrong country

In 1987 Kennedy published a book widely read as predicting American decline. In 1989 the Berlin Wall opened. In 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved, leaving the United States without a rival on earth. For a decade he was the man history had embarrassed. Except that the Soviet Union of the 1980s was the purest example anywhere of a state whose military commitments ate the economy that funded them. He had described the disease correctly and misjudged which patient would present first, which is a much smaller mistake than it looked.
take: Power is always relative, never absolute
You can improve every year and still lose position if rivals improve faster. Measure yourself against the market and the competition, not against your own last year in isolation.
Decline shows up in output, productivity and cost structure long before it shows up in dramatic events. Watch the boring numbers; they lead the exciting ones by years.
Commitments must stay smaller than the means that pay for them
Overstretch is not a lack of courage, it is an arithmetic mismatch. Every standing promise, every fixed cost, every obligation, must be sized against the base that funds it.
Britain beat France over a century and a half largely by borrowing more cheaply for longer. Whoever can access capital at the lowest cost can absorb losses that destroy a rival.
The guns, butter and investment triangle never goes away
Defending the present, satisfying people now, and building the future all compete for the same pound. Growth hides the conflict; a flat year exposes it.
The cost of staying in the same place keeps rising
Kennedy's battleship and frigate comparison generalises. In most competitive fields, holding your current standing costs more each year, so flat spending is quiet retreat.
Decline is gradual and manageable, denial is not
His actual advice was to manage erosion slowly and honestly. The expensive mistakes come from pretending the shift is not happening or trying to spend through it.
Kennedy's own verdict on his book was that it left too little room for the individual and the creative moment. Structural analysis tells you the odds, not the outcome.
title: The Boy Who Watched the Cranes Come Down
wiifm: You run a business with fixed commitments and a revenue base that moves. This is the book that explains, across five centuries and in cold numbers, why that gap is the only thing that ever really matters. You will learn why a company or a country can grow every year and still be losing, why cheap credit beats better soldiers, why the cost of simply holding your position rises relentlessly, and why the warning always appears in the boring figures years before it appears in the dramatic ones. You also get the discipline of a man who checked his own prediction, found it wrong, and said so plainly.
words: Leadership or dominance of one state or group over all the others in a system.
Kennedy's whole book is the study of bids for hegemony in Europe, from the Habsburgs onwards, and why almost all of them failed on cost.
To do with government revenue, taxation and public spending.
Britain's eighteenth century victories were a fiscal achievement before they were a military one, because the state could borrow a third of its war costs.
The gradual wearing down of strength by sustained pressure rather than by one decisive blow.
Kennedy shows that great powers are almost never knocked over; they are worn down by the slow attrition of relative economic decline.
Arranged around two dominant centres of power rather than one or many.
Two chapters of the book trace the coming of a bipolar world, in which the United States and Russia displace the older middle powers of Europe.
